lede: Not every atom of an element is the same. Chlorine atoms come in two masses, and every sample of chlorine is a mixture of both. That is why the Data Leaflet prints 35.5 for chlorine, and in this lesson you work that number out for yourself.
can: Define isotopes the way the mark scheme wants them.
Pick out isotopes from their numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons.
Calculate a relative atomic mass from mass numbers and abundances.

md: Look up chlorine on the Data Leaflet and its relative atomic mass is 35.5. No atom can hold half a proton or half a neutron, so where does the half come from? Chlorine atoms are not all the same, and 35.5 is an average of the two kinds.

prompt: In the two chlorine atoms above, which particle is present in different numbers?
explain: Neutrons: 18 in one, 20 in the other. The protons (17) and the electrons (17) are the same, which is why both are chlorine.

md: **Isotopes** are **atoms** of one element that share an **atomic number** but differ in **mass number**, because their numbers of **neutrons** differ. Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 both have 17 protons; one has 18 neutrons and the other 20.

title: Where this mark goes
md: Summer 2025 built its six-mark question on these two isotopes. Many Higher answers described a single atom, when isotopes are always plural, and Foundation answers that brought electrons into the definition lost the mark.

title: Why isotopes react in exactly the same way
md: Chemical reactions are about electrons. Isotopes have the same number of protons, so their atoms have the same number of electrons, arranged the same way: 2,8,7 for both kinds of chlorine. Only their masses differ.

prompt: Which of these is the best definition of isotopes?
options: atoms of one element that share an atomic number but differ in mass number
an atom with a different number of neutrons
atoms of an element with different numbers of electrons
answer: atoms of one element that share an atomic number but differ in mass number
explain: Plural, tied to the atomic number, and about mass numbers or neutrons. A single atom cannot be isotopes on its own, and electrons do not belong in the definition.

md: To find isotopes in a table, look for rows with the **same number of protons**: same protons, same element. Then check that their **neutrons differ**. A particle whose electrons do not match its protons is an **ion**, not an isotope. Rows with different numbers of protons are different elements, however close their masses.

prompt: In the table above, which two particles are isotopes of the same element?
explain: A and C both have 6 protons, so both are carbon, and their neutrons differ: 6 and 8. A and E share 6 neutrons, but a shared neutron count means nothing; the protons decide the element.

md:
Every sample of chlorine is a mixture: **75%** of its atoms are chlorine-35 and **25%** are chlorine-37. The **relative atomic mass**, $A_r$, compares an atom's mass with a carbon-12 atom, taken as exactly 12. For a mixture of isotopes it is a **weighted mean**: each mass number counts in proportion to how common it is.
For 100 atoms: 75 × 35 = 2625 and 25 × 37 = 925, 3550 in all. Shared over 100 atoms: 3550 ÷ 100 = **35.5**.

title: PhET: Isotopes and Atomic Mass

prompt: A sample of chlorine is 75% chlorine-35. More chlorine-37 is mixed in. What happens to the relative atomic mass of the sample?
explain: The heavier isotope now makes up more of the mixture, so the weighted mean moves towards 37. 35.5 is only right for the natural mix.

md:
**Higher tier only.** **The question.** Copper is 69% copper-63 and 31% copper-65. Calculate its relative atomic mass to 1 decimal place. **[3]**
**Step 1 — multiply each mass number by its abundance, and add.** 63 × 69 + 65 × 31 = 4347 + 2015 = **6362**. This is the top line, and every isotope must be in it.
**Step 2 — divide by 100**, because the abundances are percentages: 6362 ÷ 100 = 63.62.

prompt: Step 3 of the copper example: round 63.62 to 1 decimal place, as the question asks. What do you write?
explain: 63.6. Give the accuracy the stem asks for: in Summer 2025, C1 answers that ignored an instruction to give one decimal place lost a mark.

alt: A number line from 63 to 65. A filled dot at 63.62 is labelled 63.6, weighted mean; a hollow dot at 64 is labelled plain average.

md: Two checks catch nearly every slip. The answer must lie **between the lightest and heaviest isotope**, and **nearer the more common one**. A four-figure answer such as 6362 means the division by 100 was left out; an answer exactly halfway, 64, means the abundances were ignored.

title: GCSE Chemistry Revision "Relative Atomic Mass"
why: A second explanation of isotopes and of the relative atomic mass calculation.

prompt: Boron is 20% boron-10 and 80% boron-11. Without calculating, which value could be its relative atomic mass?
explain: 10.8: between 10 and 11, and nearer 11, the more common isotope. 10.5 ignores the abundances, 10.2 pairs them with the wrong isotopes, and 1080 was never divided by 100.

md:
define **isotopes**: atoms of one element that share an atomic number but differ in mass number.
spot isotopes in a table: same protons, different neutrons.
explain why chlorine's $A_r$ is 35.5: a weighted mean of 35 and 37.
(Higher) calculate $A_r$: multiply each mass number by its abundance, add, divide by 100, round as asked.
check that an answer lies between the isotopes and nearer the commonest.

Isotopes sit inside the atomic structure question, usually Question 1 or 2, and in Summer 2025 they carried the six-mark QWC. The first mark is the definition, in the plural; at Higher the last marks are a relative atomic mass to one decimal place. Stuck on the calculation? Multiply, add, divide by 100, then check the answer sits between the isotopes. The Sheet below lists the traps.
